{{short description|Concept in complex analysis}}
[[Image:Domain of holomorphy illustration.svg|thumb|right|The sets in the definition.]]
In [[mathematics]], in the theory of functions of [[Function of several complex variables|several complex variables]], a '''domain of holomorphy''' is a domain that is maximal in the sense that there exists a [[holomorphic function]] on this domain that cannot be [[analytic continuation|extended]] to a bigger domain.

Formally, an [[open set]] <math>\Omega</math> in the {{tmath|n}}-dimensional complex space <math>{\mathbb{C}}^n</math> is called a ''domain of holomorphy'' if there do not exist non-empty open sets  <math>U \subset \Omega</math> and  <math>V \subset {\mathbb{C}}^n</math> where <math>V</math> is [[connected space|connected]],  <math>V \not\subset \Omega</math> and  <math>U \subset \Omega \cap V</math> such that for every [[holomorphic function]] <math>f</math> on {{tmath|\Omega}}, there exists a holomorphic function <math>g</math> on <math>V</math> with <math>f = g</math> on {{tmath|U}}.

Equivalently, for any such {{tmath|U}} and {{tmath|V}}, there exists a holomorphic <math>f</math> on {{tmath|\Omega}}, such that <math>f|_U</math> cannot be analytically continued to {{tmath|V}}.

In the case {{tmath|1= n=1 }}, every open set is a domain of holomorphy: we can define a holomorphic function that is not identically zero, but whose zeros [[accumulation point|accumulate]] everywhere on the [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] of the domain, which must then be a [[analytic continuation#Natural boundary|natural boundary]] for a domain of definition of its reciprocal. For <math>n \geq 2</math> this is no longer true, as it follows from [[Hartogs's extension theorem]].

== Equivalent conditions ==
For a domain <math>\Omega</math> the following conditions are equivalent:
# <math>\Omega</math> is a domain of holomorphy.
# <math>\Omega</math> is [[holomorphically convex hull|holomorphically convex]].
# There exists a function holomorphic on <math>\Omega</math> that cannot be analytically continued beyond {{tmath|\Omega}}. That is, its domain of existence is {{tmath|\Omega}}.
# <math>\Omega</math> is [[pseudoconvex]].
# <math>\Omega</math> is '''Levi convex''' – for every sequence <math>S_{n} \subseteq \Omega</math> of analytic compact surfaces such that <math>S_{n} \rightarrow S, \partial S_{n} \rightarrow \Gamma</math> for some set <math>\Gamma</math> we have <math>S \subseteq \Omega</math> ({{tmath|\partial \Omega}} cannot be "touched from inside" by a sequence of analytic surfaces).
# <math>\Omega</math> has '''local Levi property''' – for every point <math>x \in \partial \Omega</math> there exists a neighbourhood <math>U</math> of <math>x</math> and <math>f</math> holomorphic on <math>U \cap \Omega</math> such that <math>f</math> cannot be extended to any neighbourhood of <math>x</math>
Implications <math>1 \Leftrightarrow 2 \Leftrightarrow 3, 4 \Leftrightarrow 5, 1 \Rightarrow 5, 4 \Rightarrow 6</math> are standard results (for {{tmath|1\Rightarrow 4}}, see ''[[Oka's lemma]]''). The equivalence of 1, 2, 3 is the Cartan–Thullen theorem.<ref>{{citation |last=Noguchi |first=Junjiro |chapter=Domains of Holomorphy |date=2024 |title=Basic Oka Theory in Several Complex Variables |pages=73–129 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-981-97-2056-9_3 |place=Singapore |publisher=Springer Nature Singapore |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-981-97-2056-9_3 |isbn=978-981-97-2055-2 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> The main difficulty lies in proving {{tmath|6 \Rightarrow 1}}, i.e. constructing a global holomorphic function that admits no extension from non-extendable functions defined only locally. This is called the [[Levi problem]] (after [[Eugenio Elia Levi|E. E. Levi]]) and was first solved by [[Kiyoshi Oka]], and then by [[Lars Hörmander]] using methods from [[functional analysis]] and partial differential equations (a consequence of [[D-bar problem|<math>\bar{\partial}</math>-problem]]).

== Properties ==
* If <math>\Omega_1, \dots, \Omega_{n}</math> are domains of holomorphy, then their intersection <math>\textstyle \Omega = \bigcap_{j=1}^{n} \Omega_j</math> is also a domain of holomorphy.
* If <math>\Omega_{1} \subseteq \Omega_{2} \subseteq \dots</math> is an ascending sequence of domains of holomorphy, then their union <math>\textstyle \Omega = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\Omega_{n}</math> is also a domain of holomorphy (see ''[[Behnke–Stein theorem]]'').
* If <math>\Omega_{1}</math> and  <math>\Omega_{2}</math> are domains of holomorphy, then <math> \Omega_{1} \times \Omega_{2}</math> is a domain of holomorphy.
* The first [[Cousin problems|Cousin problem]] is always solvable in a domain of holomorphy; this is also true, with additional topological assumptions, for the second [[Cousin problems|Cousin problem]].

== Examples ==
[[File:Lacunary_domain_coloring.png|thumb|Domain coloring of the 128th partial sum of the lacunary function {{tmath|1=\textstyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty z^{2^n} }}]]
<math>{\mathbb{C}}^n</math> is trivially a domain of holomorphy.

In the <math>n=1</math> case, every open set is a domain of holomorphy. A particular example is the open [[unit disk]]. Define the [[lacunary function]] {{tmath|1= \textstyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty z^{2^n} }}.

it is holomorphic on the open unit disk by the [[Weierstrass M-test]], and singular at all {{tmath| \{e^{2i\pi k/2^n} : n, k \in \N\} }}, which is dense on the unit circle, and therefore it cannot be analytically extended beyond the unit disk.

In the <math>n \geq 2</math> case, let <math>K \subset U \subset \mathbb C^n</math> where <math>U</math> is open and <math>K</math> is nonempty and compact. If <math>U \setminus K</math> is connected, then by the [[Hartogs's extension theorem]], any function holomorphic on <math>U \setminus K</math> can be analytically continued to {{tmath|U}}, which means <math>U \setminus K</math> is an open set that is not a domain of holomorphy. Thus, domain of holomorphy becomes a nontrivial concept in the case {{tmath| n \geq 2 }}.
